MULTICULTURALISM: THE FAILED UNIPARTY EXPERIMENT. WHERE’S THE FIX?

A shared country requires a willingness to belong to it. Government must answer for the results.

By Steve English  |  19 October 2026

If you choose to make Britain your home, you should want to become part of Britain.

You should have respect for its people, an interest in its history and a willingness to embrace its traditions and way of life. Making your home here should mean joining the country and contributing to its future.

Britain is entitled to expect that commitment.

Settling here should never be treated as an opportunity to build a separate society, reject the freedoms that attracted you or pursue a political project to impose religious rule on everybody else. Seeking power through numbers does not make the removal of other people’s freedoms acceptable.

Everyone should be free to keep family traditions and practise their faith. That freedom comes with an equal obligation to respect the choices of others—including their right to disagree, criticise religion or live without it.

Britain’s laws can change through democratic debate. But equal citizenship, freedom of conscience and protection from coercion must apply to everyone. No community gets to reserve those rights for itself while denying them to its neighbours.

Government should say this clearly. It should expect people settling here to learn English, participate in the wider community and accept the same rights and responsibilities as everyone else.

And it should challenge those who deliberately encourage isolation or demand control over other people’s lives.

A shared country requires a willingness to belong to it. Yet governments have repeatedly admitted that their policies encouraged people to live apart.

That is where this failure begins—and where political accountability must start.

They knew there was a problem

In February 2011, David Cameron criticised state multiculturalism in his Munich Security Conference speech. He said government had encouraged separate lives and failed to provide a shared national identity. He also acknowledged the toleration of behaviour that contradicted the country’s values. [1]

Those were the words of a Conservative prime minister.

Once a government makes that admission, it takes responsibility for putting things right. Identifying a failure from a lectern is the easy part. Changing policy, challenging entrenched interests and defending people whose freedoms are being restricted require action.

Five years later, another official review was describing serious problems.

The warnings kept coming

The government-commissioned Casey Review, published in December 2016, found increasing ethnic segregation in some areas and insufficient attention to integration alongside the pace and scale of population change. It also identified serious inequalities affecting women in some communities. [2]

Its findings concerned everyday life: access to work, the ability to speak English, opportunities to mix and the freedom to make personal decisions.

The review highlighted coercive control, violence and abuse committed in the name of cultural or religious values. Its recommendations included English teaching, greater contact between communities and clearer expectations for people coming to settle. [2]

These were matters of freedom, safety and opportunity.

A woman unable to seek help without someone speaking for her needs practical support. A child whose future is being restricted needs adults prepared to intervene. Someone threatened for rejecting a religious belief needs protection.

Calling a practice cultural does not remove the harm it causes.

Rights belong to individuals

Government should deal with citizens as people with their own views and rights.

A community leader cannot be assumed to speak for every woman, every young person or every dissenter in the neighbourhood. Officials who rely too heavily on approved spokespeople risk hearing least from those who most need help.

People must be able to choose their partners, pursue education, take employment and decide what they believe.

Those freedoms need to exist inside the home and community as well as on a government website.

Religious organisations should be free to persuade. They should have no power to compel. Anyone seeking compulsory religious government should face clear political opposition, whatever faith they invoke.

The same standard must apply throughout Britain.

Integration needs expectations—and opportunities

Learning English should be a clear expectation for those making a permanent home here. Government should provide an effective route to doing so.

Parents need to communicate with schools. Workers need access to jobs. Patients need to explain their symptoms. Neighbours need to be able to talk to each other.

Language is part of independence.

Integration also requires places where people meet: schools, workplaces, clubs, public spaces and local activities. A policy that measures success only by how many people have arrived or received documents misses the essential question: are people becoming part of a shared society?

The Casey Review called for more mixing between communities and greater support for English language learning. Those are practical tasks against which government can be judged. [2]

The numbers cannot be ignored

Ministers deciding immigration policy must account for the capacity of the places receiving people.

Homes have to be available. Schools need places and staff. Health services need capacity. Language teaching and integration support need funding.

Government cannot make national decisions and leave individual neighbourhoods to absorb every consequence.

The Casey Review explicitly called for greater integration efforts in response to the pace and scale of immigration and population change. [2]

Residents are entitled to ask how much change their area can manage, what support will accompany it and whether ministers have a credible plan.

Those questions deserve answers backed by figures and resources.

Children deserve a wider future

Being born in Britain should bring a real opportunity to participate fully in its life.

Children growing up with little contact outside an isolated community need access to wider friendships, education and employment. They should be able to decide their futures without intimidation from anyone claiming authority over them.

Poverty, poor housing and limited educational opportunities also create barriers. Parliament’s scrutiny of the Casey Review raised precisely these concerns about the need to examine wider social problems. [3]

A serious government must tackle those barriers alongside coercive practices and deliberate isolation.

Every child deserves the chance to belong, succeed and make choices.

Britain should be clear about what it offers

Britain offers freedoms worth defending: democratic government, open debate, freedom of worship, freedom from religious compulsion and equal protection under the law.

Its history deserves to be taught honestly, with its achievements and failures examined. Its traditions deserve to be understood and enjoyed. Its people deserve respect.

Newcomers should be invited into that shared life with clear expectations and a fair opportunity to participate.

Anyone encouraging permanent separation should be challenged. Anyone threatening others should face the consequences. Public bodies should defend the individual whose rights are being violated, even when doing so upsets an influential organisation or spokesman.

So who is proposing to fix it?

After all those warnings, voters deserve to know what the parties actually propose.

There are proposals. The question is whether they address the problem—and whether the parties making them can be trusted to deliver.

Labour: another strategy, with promises to enforce expectations

Labour’s government has published plans for national integration expectations, a government-wide integration strategy and a review of English teaching.

Its programme includes stronger expectations around language, work and participation, an updated Life in the UK test and a proposed ten-year standard route to settlement, with adjustments for contribution. Several integration measures apply specifically to England; immigration and settlement policy operate across the UK. [4]

Those commitments should be measured against results. How many people gain usable English? Are isolated women becoming more independent? Are schools and neighbourhoods becoming less divided?

Publishing another strategy cannot count as completing the job.

Conservatives: promising to dismantle what failed on their watch

Kemi Badenoch has proposed an Integration and Cohesion Plan, common standards across public bodies, changes to the school curriculum, stronger protection for free speech and an overhaul of the Equality Act. She has also commissioned work on Islamist extremism and separatism. Parts of this programme remain proposals for reviews and policy development. [5]

The Conservatives are entitled to put forward new policies. Voters are equally entitled to remember their record.

Cameron acknowledged the problem in 2011. His party remained in government until 2024.

Why should the public believe that another Conservative administration would deliver what previous Conservative administrations failed to secure?

Remember who has been in charge

Labour and the Conservatives have alternated in leading Britain’s governments for more than a century. These are the two parties we mean when we talk about the Uniparty.

Between them, they shaped the immigration and integration policies that brought us here. Both have had opportunities to change course. Both must answer for the failures identified in their own government speeches and official reviews.

Now they offer fresh promises to repair the divisions that developed under their leadership.

The public is entitled to ask why the parties responsible for overseeing this failure should be trusted to fix it this time.

Reform UK: immigration controls alongside cultural commitments

Reform’s proposals relevant to this argument cover both immigration and the country’s public institutions.

Its current immigration platform includes net negative migration; replacing Indefinite Leave to Remain, including rescinding existing awards, with renewable five-year visas; higher salary requirements; English fluency; stronger character tests; and work visas focused on critical shortages, with caps and requirements to train British workers. It also proposes welfare restrictions for foreign nationals, with distinctions and pension provisions set out in its policy. [6]

On illegal immigration, Operation Fortress proposes intercepting Channel crossings and returning those aboard to France or Belgium. Operation Restoring Justice proposes a five-year identification, detention and deportation programme, a Deportation Command, additional detention capacity, return agreements and visa sanctions against countries refusing returns. Reform also proposes leaving the European Convention on Human Rights and repealing the Human Rights Act. These are proposed measures, not arrangements already secured with other governments. [6]

Its social housing policy proposes ending access for foreign nationals and removing existing foreign-national tenants after a grace period, alongside building 50,000 additional affordable homes a year. [7]

Its 2024 Contract contained commitments directly relevant to national identity and public freedoms: replacing the Equality Act; scrapping specified diversity, equality and inclusion rules; introducing a comprehensive Free Speech Bill; stopping the use of Sharia law in the UK; promoting British culture, identity and values; making St George’s Day and St David’s Day public holidays; and developing education that builds knowledge of Britain and pride in the country. [8]

These proposals give voters specific policies to examine. They also leave practical questions that deserve answers: how rights would be protected under replacement legislation, how religious coercion would be distinguished from voluntary worship, and how existing isolated communities would be helped into wider British life.

Reducing immigration can change the pace of future arrivals. Overcoming established separation also requires schools, language teaching, employment, policing and protection for individuals.

The test is delivery

Every party should face the same questions.

Will people settling here be expected to learn the language and participate in British life? Will women and dissenters receive protection when they challenge controlling community figures? Will public authorities defend free expression and apply common standards consistently?

And will immigration decisions reflect the capacity of the communities expected to accommodate them?

Britain deserves a government prepared to set those expectations, defend those freedoms and answer for the results.

The parties that governed through these failures owe the public an explanation. Those offering a different course owe the public a workable plan.
